newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-BOWE-GOLOTA SET FOR DECEMBER IN ATLANTIC CITY.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-BOWE-GOLOTA SET FOR DECEMBER IN ATLANTIC CITY.

text.p: Andrew Golota says every day since his disqualification against Riddick Bowe three months ago he has thought about getting a rematch.
"I want it to beat this guy," said Golota Thursday at the News conference to formally announce the rematch December 14 in Atlantic City.

Bowe says he has been constantly reminded by his family about how badly he was getting beaten up on July 11 before Golota was disqualified in the seventh round for low blows and wants to redeem himself.

"I was there one day and my moma said you know what, Riddick, that Andrew Golota guy was kicking your ass'. She made me feel that big," said Bowe holding his finger and thumb about an inch apart. "How was I suppose to feel? I had to take it she was telling the truth.
"I have to prove to my moma that I don't need to retire," said Bowe (39-1). "I just had a bad day at the office and that I'm still the best heavyweight in the world. I want to make her feel proud."

All parties involved were on their best behaviour Thursday, a far cry from the post fight riot broke out between members of the rival camps and fans at Madison Square Garden after Golota's disqualification.
Garden officials said after the riot they would not again do business with Bowe or his manager, Rock Newman, who was singled out by many people to have contributed to the riot.

"While we can't escape the reality of the uglyness of what happened after the bell, everyone who was unfortunatley associated with that has agreed to put it behind us for good," promoter Dino Duva said of the riot that ended in several arrests and a $250,000 fine for the Bowe camp.

Golota still carries a scar atop his head after taking 13 stitches to close a gash from being clubbed with a walkie talkie during the melee. Golata said the clubbing left him with headaches for several days afterwards.
But the former Polish Olympian, who now lives in Chicago, now jokes about the incident.
"It was my fault, I should have ducked," said Golota, 28.
"I need to prove that I can beat him," said Golota. "I will do the same thing, exactly. What can he do more? He'll be the same guy."
Bowe though warned that he won't be the same fighter he was in the first fight.
"I thought he was pushover," Bowe said of Golota (28-1). "Golota embarrassed me. I was humilated. I not only have something to prove to myself, but I have something to prove to everybody."

Possibly more than anybody else Bowe has something to prove to, is his former trainer 85-year-old Eddie Futch, who severed his eight-year relationship with the fighter earlier this month. Futch said the 29-year-old Bowe had lot his focus and lacked the commitment to regain the heavyweight championship.

"I think it will be a big difference," Bowe said of fighting without the man he affectionately calls "Papa Smurf". "Over the past years I have trained myself to hear two voices, that's Papa Smurf and Rock Newman). Now there only be one voice there.
"I'm very determined, maybe because of this situation."
